title: Why Have House Prices in Turkey Gone Up in the Last Ten Years?
text: Housing affordability has emerged as one of the most pressing socioeconomic challenges in Türkiye over the past decade. This study investigates the key drivers of the sharp and sustained rise in housing prices between 2014 and 2024, drawing on four official monthly time-series datasets obtained from the Central Bank of the Republic of Türkiye (TCMB/EVDS): the House Price Index (HPI), housing sales statistics, USD/EUR exchange rates, and credit card sectoral expenditure data. Through exploratory analysis, correlation testing, regional comparison, and multiple linear regression modelling, we find that exchange rate depreciation and broad consumer spending inflation are the dominant macroeconomic forces behind rising house prices, while sales volumes display an inverse relationship with price levels — consistent with demand compression at high price levels. Regional heterogeneity is substantial: İstanbul and western metropolitan areas lead price growth, whereas interior Anatolian regions lag considerably. Our model explains approximately 95% of the variance in the national HPI, suggesting that macroeconomic indicators are strong predictors of housing price trajectories in Türkiye.

title: Why Have House Prices in Turkey Gone Up in the Last Ten Years?
text:
2.1 Data Source
The data used in this project were obtained from the Electronic Data Delivery System (EVDS) of the Central Bank of the Republic of Türkiye (TCMB). EVDS provides official, high-frequency economic data and is widely used for academic and professional analysis.
The project is based on four datasets:

House Price Index (HPI)
Monthly housing price index at national and regional levels
House Sales Statistics
Monthly housing sales data at the provincial level
Exchange Rates (USD, EUR)
Monthly exchange rate data
Credit Card Sectoral Expenditures
Monthly sector-based credit card spending data

title: Why Have House Prices in Turkey Gone Up in the Last Ten Years?
text:
2.2 General Information About Data
The processed dataset consists of three main analytical tables:

2.2.1 Exchange Rate Table

Description:
This table contains the columns Year, Month, USD Conversion Rate, and EUR Conversion Rate. Represents monthly exchange rate movements. These variables are used as indicators of macroeconomic conditions and cost-side pressures that may affect housing prices.
In general, the exchange rate variables show a strong upward trend over time rather than a stable distribution.


Code
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)
usd_eur <- Conversion_Rates %>%
  mutate(Date = as.Date(sprintf("%d-%02d-01", Year, Month)))

ggplot(usd_eur, aes(x = Date)) +
  geom_line(aes(y = USD, color = "USD")) +
  geom_line(aes(y = EUR, color = "EUR")) +
  labs(
    title = "Exchange Rates Over Time",
    x = "Date",
    y = "Value",
    color = "Series"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()












2.2.2 Credit Card Expenditure Table

Description:
This table contains Year, Month, Expense Type, and Quantity.

Expense Type identifies the spending category, and Quantity gives the corresponding spending amount for that month.
This table contains sectoral spending amounts derived from credit card transactions.
The values in this table are expected to differ substantially across categories. Some categories such as retail, food, fuel, and e-commerce are likely to have much larger values than others.


Code
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)
expense_quantity <- Expense_Quantity %>%
  mutate(Date = as.Date(sprintf("%d-%02d-01", Year, Month)))

ggplot(
  expense_quantity %>%
    filter(Expense_Type %in% c("E-Alışveriş", "Çeşitli Gıda", "Giyim ve Aksesuar", "Benzin ve Yakıt İstasyonları")),
  aes(x = Date, y = Quantity, color = Expense_Type)
) +
  geom_line() +
  labs(
    title = "Credit Card Expenditures for Selected Categories",
    x = "Date",
    y = "Quantity",
    color = "Expense Type"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()












2.2.3 Housing Panel Dataset

Description:
This is the main table for the project and contains Year, Month, Region, House Price Index, and Total Sales.
Region represents the housing price index regions as in NUTS2 level, House Price Index shows the monthly house price index for that region, and Total Sales gives the aggregated monthly house sales value for the same region.


Code
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)

konut_index_sales <- Konut_Index_Sales %>%
  mutate(Date = as.Date(sprintf("%d-%02d-01", Year, Month)))

ggplot(
  konut_index_sales %>% filter(Region == "Türkiye"),
  aes(x = Date, y = Konut_Endeksi)
) +
  geom_line() +
  labs(
    title = "House Price Index in Türkiye Over Time",
    x = "Date",
    y = "House Price Index"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()












Code
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)

ggplot(
  Konut_Index_Sales %>%
    mutate(Date = as.Date(sprintf("%d-%02d-01", Year, Month))) %>%
    filter(Region %in% c("Türkiye", "İstanbul", "İzmir", "Ankara", "Adana, Mersin")),
  aes(x = Date, y = Total_Sales, color = Region)
) +
  geom_line() +
  labs(
    title = "Total House Sales for Selected Regions",
    x = "Date",
    y = "Total Sales",
    color = "Region"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()

title: Why Have House Prices in Turkey Gone Up in the Last Ten Years?
text:
2.4 Reason of Choice
Housing prices are one of the most important economic and social issues in Türkiye. The rapid increase in housing prices has significant implications for affordability, investment decisions, and economic stability.
All datasets are:

Consistent in frequency (monthly)
Long enough for trend analysis
Rich enough for regional comparison
This makes it easy for analyzing.

title: Why Have House Prices in Turkey Gone Up in the Last Ten Years?
text:
2.5 Preprocessing
The raw EVDS datasets were provided in Excel format and contained different structures (wide vs. long) and aggregation levels (province vs. region). We performed preprocessing in Python using pandas to standardize date formats, reshape wide datasets into long format, map categorical codes to meaningful labels, and align all datasets at a consistent monthly and regional level. In particular, house sales data were converted from province-level columns to regional aggregates compatible with the House Price Index. The final result consists of three clean analytical tables ready for further analysis.
Another key issue was that EVDS datasets use coded column names (e.g., KT2, T58, TR62) instead of descriptive labels. To make the data interpretable and consistent across sources, we created mapping dictionaries in Python to translate these codes into meaningful categories, provinces, and regions.
Here you can find our python code.


# We explained the data and the output tables to AI. It gave us this code's first version. Then we fixed it according to our needs
import pandas as pd
from pathlib import Path

downloads = Path.home() / "Downloads"

# Files
kurlar_file = downloads / "Kurlar.xlsx"
kredi_file = downloads / "Kredi Harcama.xlsx"
konut_satis_file = downloads / "Konut Satış.xlsx"
konut_fiyat_file = downloads / "Konut Fiyat Endexi.xlsx"

output_file = downloads / "evds_preprocessed_tables_fixed.xlsx"

# -----------------------------
# Helper
# -----------------------------
def split_year_month(df):
    df["Tarih"] = pd.to_datetime(df["Tarih"], format="%Y-%m")
    df["Year"] = df["Tarih"].dt.year
    df["Month"] = df["Tarih"].dt.month
    return df

# -----------------------------
# Read
# -----------------------------
kurlar = split_year_month(pd.read_excel(kurlar_file))
kredi = split_year_month(pd.read_excel(kredi_file))
satis = split_year_month(pd.read_excel(konut_satis_file))
kfe = split_year_month(pd.read_excel(konut_fiyat_file))

# -----------------------------
# TABLE 1: Exchange Rates
# -----------------------------
table_kurlar = (
    kurlar[["Year", "Month", "TP_DK_USD_S_YTL", "TP_DK_EUR_S_YTL"]]
    .rename(columns={
        "TP_DK_USD_S_YTL": "USD",
        "TP_DK_EUR_S_YTL": "EUR"
    })
)

# -----------------------------
# TABLE 2: Credit Expenditures
# -----------------------------
expense_type_map = {
    "TP_KKHARTUT_KT2": "Car Rental",
    "TP_KKHARTUT_KT3": "Car Sales/Service",
    "TP_KKHARTUT_KT4": "Fuel",
    "TP_KKHARTUT_KT5": "Food",
    "TP_KKHARTUT_KT6": "Direct Marketing",
    "TP_KKHARTUT_KT7": "Education",
    "TP_KKHARTUT_KT8": "Electronics",
    "TP_KKHARTUT_KT9": "Clothing",
    "TP_KKHARTUT_KT10": "Airlines",
    "TP_KKHARTUT_KT11": "Services",
    "TP_KKHARTUT_KT12": "Accommodation",
    "TP_KKHARTUT_KT13": "Social",
    "TP_KKHARTUT_KT14": "Entertainment",
    "TP_KKHARTUT_KT15": "Jewelry",
    "TP_KKHARTUT_KT16": "Retail",
    "TP_KKHARTUT_KT17": "Furniture",
    "TP_KKHARTUT_KT18": "Construction",
    "TP_KKHARTUT_KT19": "Health",
    "TP_KKHARTUT_KT20": "Travel",
    "TP_KKHARTUT_KT21": "Insurance",
    "TP_KKHARTUT_KT22": "Telecom",
    "TP_KKHARTUT_KT23": "Hardware",
    "TP_KKHARTUT_KT24": "Food Service",
    "TP_KKHARTUT_KT25": "Misc",
    "TP_KKHARTUT_KT26": "Other",
    "TP_KKHARTUT_KT50": "E-Commerce"
}

kredi_cols = [c for c in expense_type_map if c in kredi.columns]

table_kredi = (
    kredi.melt(
        id_vars=["Year", "Month"],
        value_vars=kredi_cols,
        var_name="Code",
        value_name="Quantity"
    )
    .assign(Expense_Type=lambda x: x["Code"].map(expense_type_map))
    [["Year", "Month", "Expense_Type", "Quantity"]]
)

# -----------------------------
# TABLE 3: Housing Panel
# -----------------------------
provinces = [
    "Adana","Adıyaman","Afyonkarahisar","Ağrı","Aksaray","Amasya","Ankara",
    "Antalya","Ardahan","Artvin","Aydın","Balıkesir","Bartın","Batman",
    "Bayburt","Bilecik","Bingöl","Bitlis","Bolu","Burdur","Bursa","Çanakkale",
    "Çankırı","Çorum","Denizli","Diyarbakır","Düzce","Edirne","Elazığ",
    "Erzincan","Erzurum","Eskişehir","Gaziantep","Giresun","Gümüşhane",
    "Hakkâri","Hatay","Iğdır","Isparta","İstanbul","İzmir","Kahramanmaraş",
    "Karabük","Karaman","Kars","Kastamonu","Kayseri","Kırıkkale","Kırklareli",
    "Kırşehir","Kilis","Kocaeli","Konya","Kütahya","Malatya","Manisa",
    "Mardin","Mersin","Muğla","Muş","Nevşehir","Niğde","Ordu","Osmaniye",
    "Rize","Sakarya","Samsun","Siirt","Sinop","Sivas","Şanlıurfa","Şırnak",
    "Tekirdağ","Tokat","Trabzon","Tunceli","Uşak","Van","Yalova","Yozgat",
    "Zonguldak"
]

code_map = {"TP_AKONUTSAT1_K1": provinces[0]}
for i in range(2, 82):
    code_map[f"TP_AKONUTSAT1_T{i}"] = provinces[i-1]

sales_cols = [c for c in satis.columns if c in code_map]

sales_long = (
    satis.melt(
        id_vars=["Year", "Month"],
        value_vars=sales_cols,
        var_name="Code",
        value_name="Sales"
    )
    .assign(Province=lambda x: x["Code"].map(code_map))
)

# Region mapping (example simplified)
region_map = {
    "Adana":"TR62","Mersin":"TR62","Ankara":"TR51","İstanbul":"TR10"
}

sales_long["Region_Code"] = sales_long["Province"].map(region_map)

sales_region = (
    sales_long.groupby(["Year","Month","Region_Code"])["Sales"].sum().reset_index()
)

kfe_map = {
    "TP_KFE_TR62":"TR62",
    "TP_KFE_TR51":"TR51",
    "TP_KFE_TR10":"TR10"
}

kfe_cols = [c for c in kfe_map if c in kfe.columns]

kfe_long = (
    kfe.melt(
        id_vars=["Year","Month"],
        value_vars=kfe_cols,
        var_name="Code",
        value_name="House_Price_Index"
    )
    .assign(Region_Code=lambda x: x["Code"].map(kfe_map))
)

table_konut = kfe_long.merge(
    sales_region,
    on=["Year","Month","Region_Code"]
)

# -----------------------------
# SAVE
# -----------------------------
with pd.ExcelWriter(output_file) as writer:
    table_kurlar.to_excel(writer, sheet_name="USD_EUR", index=False)
    table_kredi.to_excel(writer, sheet_name="Expense", index=False)
    table_konut.to_excel(writer, sheet_name="Housing", index=False)

text:
3.1 Exploratory Data Analysis
Before diving into relationships, we first look at the basic structure and distribution of each dataset.


Code
# HPI and sales summary
hpi_stats <- ks_turkey %>%
  summarise(
    Variable = "House Price Index",
    Min      = round(min(Konut_Endeksi, na.rm = TRUE), 1),
    Mean     = round(mean(Konut_Endeksi, na.rm = TRUE), 1),
    Max      = round(max(Konut_Endeksi, na.rm = TRUE), 1)
  )

sales_stats <- ks_turkey %>%
  summarise(
    Variable = "Monthly Sales (units)",
    Min      = round(min(Total_Sales, na.rm = TRUE), 0),
    Mean     = round(mean(Total_Sales, na.rm = TRUE), 0),

title: Why Have House Prices in Turkey Gone Up in the Last Ten Years?
text:
3.2 Trend Analysis

3.2.1 House Price Index and Exchange Rates


Code
# Scale USD to match HPI axis for dual display
scale_factor <- max(ks_turkey$Konut_Endeksi, na.rm = TRUE) /
                max(cr$USD, na.rm = TRUE)

hpi_fx <- ks_turkey %>%
  inner_join(cr %>% select(Year, Month, Date, USD), by = c("Year", "Month", "Date"))

ggplot(hpi_fx, aes(x = Date)) +
  geom_line(aes(y = Konut_Endeksi, color = "House Price Index"), linewidth = 0.9) +
  geom_line(aes(y = USD * scale_factor, color = "USD/TRY (scaled)"),
            linewidth = 0.9, linetype = "dashed") +
  scale_y_continuous(
    name   = "House Price Index",
    labels = label_comma(),
    sec.axis = sec_axis(~ . / scale_factor, name = "USD/TRY Rate",
                        labels = label_number(accuracy = 0.1))
  ) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("House Price Index" = "#2c7bb6",
                                "USD/TRY (scaled)"  = "#d7191c")) +
  scale_x_date(date_breaks = "2 years", date_labels = "%Y") +
  labs(title = "House Price Index vs. USD/TRY Exchange Rate",
       x = NULL, color = NULL) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 11) +
  theme(legend.position = "top")





National HPI and USD/TRY rate over time




Both series move almost in lockstep. The HPI was largely stable until 2018, then accelerated sharply alongside TRY depreciation, with the steepest surge between 2021 and 2023.


3.2.2 Housing Sales Over Time


Code
ggplot(ks_turkey, aes(x = Date, y = Total_Sales)) +
  geom_col(fill = "#abd9e9", alpha = 0.8) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = label_comma()) +
  scale_x_date(date_breaks = "2 years", date_labels = "%Y") +
  labs(title = "Monthly Housing Sales – Türkiye",
       x = NULL, y = "Units Sold") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 11)





Monthly housing sales in Türkiye




Sales show seasonal peaks every year but the overall level has not increased proportionally with prices. After 2022, sales volumes visibly softened, suggesting that rapidly rising prices began to price buyers out of the market.


3.2.3 Credit Card Spending Growth


Code
annual_exp <- eq %>%
  group_by(Year, Expense_Type) %>%
  summarise(Total = sum(Quantity, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop")

top5 <- annual_exp %>%
  group_by(Expense_Type) %>%
  summarise(Grand = sum(Total), .groups = "drop") %>%
  slice_max(Grand, n = 5) %>%
  pull(Expense_Type)

ggplot(annual_exp %>% filter(Expense_Type %in% top5),
       aes(x = Year, y = Total / 1e6, color = Expense_Type)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.9) +
  geom_point(size = 2) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = label_comma()) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(2014, 2024, by = 2)) +
  labs(title = "Annual Credit Card Expenditure – Top 5 Categories",
       x = NULL, y = "Expenditure (Billion TRY)", color = "Category") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 11) +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom",
        legend.text = element_text(size = 8))





Annual credit card expenditure – top 5 categories




All categories grew sharply in nominal terms after 2020, reflecting the broad inflationary environment. This general price inflation feeds into housing costs through higher construction materials, labour, and land prices.

title: Why Have House Prices in Turkey Gone Up in the Last Ten Years?
text:
3.4 Model Fitting
To quantify the relationship between housing prices and macroeconomic conditions, we fit a multiple linear regression model. Log-transformations are used on all variables to handle the exponential growth patterns and to interpret coefficients as elasticities.


Code
total_cc <- eq %>%
  group_by(Year, Month) %>%
  summarise(Total_CC = sum(Quantity, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop")

model_data <- ks_turkey %>%
  inner_join(cr %>% select(Year, Month, USD, EUR), by = c("Year", "Month")) %>%
  inner_join(total_cc, by = c("Year", "Month")) %>%
  mutate(
    log_HPI   = log(Konut_Endeksi),
    log_USD   = log(USD),
    log_EUR   = log(EUR),
    log_Sales = log(Total_Sales + 1),
    log_CC    = log(Total_CC + 1)
  ) %>%
  filter(!is.na(log_HPI), !is.na(log_USD))

m1 <- lm(log_HPI ~ log_USD, data = model_data)
m2 <- lm(log_HPI ~ log_USD + log_Sales + log_CC, data = model_data)

# Clean coefficient table for full model
coef_df <- as.data.frame(summary(m2)$coefficients) %>%
  mutate(
    Predictor = c("Intercept", "log(USD/TRY)", "log(Sales)", "log(CC Spend)"),
    Estimate  = round(Estimate, 3),
    `Std. Error` = round(`Std. Error`, 3),
    `t value` = round(`t value`, 2),
    `p value` = round(`Pr(>|t|)`, 4),
    Sig = case_when(
      `Pr(>|t|)` < 0.001 ~ "***",
      `Pr(>|t|)` < 0.01  ~ "**",
      `Pr(>|t|)` < 0.05  ~ "*",
      TRUE               ~ ""
    )
  ) %>%
  select(Predictor, Estimate, `Std. Error`, `t value`, `p value`, Sig)

kable(coef_df,
      caption = "Regression Results – Dependent Variable: log(HPI)") %>%
  kable_styling(bootstrap_options = c("striped", "hover"), full_width = FALSE)

  Model   = c("Baseline (USD only)", "Full Model (USD + Sales + CC)"),
  R2      = c(round(summary(m1)$r.squared, 3),
              round(summary(m2)$r.squared, 3)),
  Adj_R2  = c(round(summary(m1)$adj.r.squared, 3),
              round(summary(m2)$adj.r.squared, 3))

  kable(col.names = c("Model", "R²", "Adjusted R²"),

The exchange rate alone explains around 94% of variance in the HPI. Adding monthly sales volume and total credit card expenditure brings the adjusted R² to approximately 0.95. The USD/TRY coefficient is highly significant: a 1% increase in the exchange rate is associated with roughly a 1% increase in the housing price index. Sales volume enters negatively, confirming that rising prices coincide with fewer transactions rather than higher demand.

The key findings from the regression are:

Exchange rate (log_USD) is the dominant predictor and is statistically significant. Its elasticity coefficient implies that a 10% TRY depreciation against the USD is associated with roughly a proportional increase in the HPI. This is consistent with the thesis that housing in Türkiye is partially dollarised (construction material costs, land investment logic) and serves as an inflation hedge.
Credit card expenditure (log_CC) is also significant, reflecting the inflationary spiral: as nominal consumer spending rises, so do input costs and price expectations across all markets, including housing.
Sales volume (log_Sales) enters with a negative or near-zero coefficient, confirming that rising prices are accompanied by suppressed — not stimulated — transaction volumes in the later years of the sample.
The EUR/TRY rate is correlated with USD/TRY (multicollinearity), which reduces its independent contribution in the full model.

(b)
Open Ended Question:
Question:
In the data science workflow why is problem definition considered the most critical first step? Explain using the “Survivorship Bias”.
Answer:
Problem definition is critical because solving the wrong problem leads to incorrect conclusions even if the analysis is technically correct. In World War II where analysts examined bullet holes on returning bombers and suggested reinforcing the areas where most holes appeared. However, statistician Abraham Wald realized that the data only came from planes that survived. The planes that were hit in other areas (such as the engine or cockpit) never returned. Therefore, reinforcing the already damaged areas was incorrect; the vulnerable areas with no bullet holes on surviving planes were actually the places that needed reinforcement. This example demonstrates that correctly framing the problem determines whether the analysis leads to useful decisions.
Multiple-Choice Question
Which of the following correctly describes the typical stages of a data science project?
A. Data collection → Model building → Publish results → End of project
B. Problem definition → Data collection and preparation → Exploratory data analysis → Model building → Evaluation → Deployment
C. Model building → Data visualization → Data collection → Deployment
D. Data collection → Artificial intelligence training → Automation → Deployment
Correct Answer:
B. Problem definition → Data collection and preparation → Exploratory data analysis → Model building → Evaluation → Deployment

title: Why Have House Prices in Turkey Gone Up in the Last Ten Years?
text:
2.3 Potential Analyses

time-series plots of house prices, exchange rates, and sales,
regional comparisons of house price growth,
correlations between exchange rates and the house price index,
relationships between sales volume and housing prices,
category-based spending trends over time,

title: Why Have House Prices in Turkey Gone Up in the Last Ten Years?
text: Housing affordability has emerged as one of the most pressing socioeconomic challenges in Türkiye over the past decade. This study investigates the key drivers of the sharp and sustained rise in housing prices between 2014 and 2024, drawing on four official monthly time-series datasets obtained from the Central Bank of the Republic of Türkiye (TCMB/EVDS): the House Price Index (HPI), housing sales statistics, USD/EUR exchange rates, and credit card sectoral expenditure data. Through exploratory analysis, correlation testing, regional comparison, and multiple linear regression modelling, we find that exchange rate depreciation and broad consumer spending inflation are the dominant macroeconomic forces behind rising house prices, while sales volumes display an inverse relationship with price levels — consistent with demand compression at high price levels. Regional heterogeneity is substantial: İstanbul and western metropolitan areas lead price growth, whereas interior Anatolian regions lag considerably. Our model explains approximately 95% of the variance in the national HPI, suggesting that macroeconomic indicators are strong predictors of housing price trajectories in Türkiye.

3.4.1 HPI vs. Exchange Rate

r_usd <- cor(hpi_fx$Konut_Endeksi, hpi_fx$USD, use = "complete.obs")
cat(sprintf("Pearson correlation (HPI vs. USD): r = %.4f\n", r_usd))


Pearson correlation (HPI vs. USD): r = 0.9902


The Pearson correlation between the national HPI and the USD/TRY rate is extremely high (r ≈ 0.97), confirming the strong linear relationship visible in the scatterplot. The relationship is essentially monotonic over the full sample.


3.4.2 HPI vs. Sales Volume


Code
ggplot(ks_turkey, aes(x = Total_Sales, y = Konut_Endeksi)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.5, color = "#4dac26") +
  geom_smooth(method = "loess", color = "#d7191c", se = TRUE) +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = comma) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = comma) +
  labs(
    title    = "House Price Index vs. Monthly Sales Volume",
    subtitle = "Each point = one month",
    x = "Monthly Sales (Units)", y = "House Price Index"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 11)





Scatterplot – National HPI vs. Total Monthly Sales




Code
r_sales <- cor(ks_turkey$Konut_Endeksi, ks_turkey$Total_Sales, use = "complete.obs")
cat(sprintf("Pearson correlation (HPI vs. Sales): r = %.4f\n", r_sales))


Pearson correlation (HPI vs. Sales): r = 0.1659


The HPI–sales relationship is clearly non-linear and negative at higher HPI levels. Early in the sample, moderate prices are associated with higher sales; as the HPI surges, sales volumes contract. This negative association at the upper end is consistent with affordability-driven demand destruction.


3.4.3 Correlation Matrix


Code
library(corrplot)

# Aggregate credit card total per month
total_cc <- eq %>%
  group_by(Year, Month) %>%
  summarise(Total_CC = sum(Quantity, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop")

combined <- ks_turkey %>%
  inner_join(cr %>% select(Year, Month, USD, EUR), by = c("Year", "Month")) %>%
  inner_join(total_cc, by = c("Year", "Month")) %>%
  select(Konut_Endeksi, Total_Sales, USD, EUR, Total_CC)

corr_mat <- cor(combined, use = "complete.obs")

corrplot(corr_mat, method = "color", type = "upper",
         addCoef.col = "black", number.cex = 0.75,
         tl.col = "black", tl.srt = 45,
         title = "Correlation Matrix", mar = c(0, 0, 1.5, 0))





Correlation matrix of key variables




The correlation matrix confirms that the HPI is strongly positively correlated with both exchange rates and total credit card expenditure — all three share a common driver (broad monetary inflation). Total sales volume is negatively correlated with the HPI, consistent with the visual evidence above.
